When two parties are in a discussion and one asserts a claim that the other disputes, the one who asserts has a burden of proof to justify or substantiate that claim. An argument from ignorance occurs when either a proposition is assumed to be true because it has not yet been proved false or a proposition is assumed to be false because it has not yet been proved true. This shifts the burden of proof to the person criticizing the proposition.

A few things that mitigate this:

* A lot of employers will pay more than the minimum contribution. In my job, my employer pays 5% and I pay 3%. I can't remember the exact terms of auto-enrolment minimum contributions, but that's fairly typical.

* Online pension calculators are usually pretty misleading, often predicting very low rates of growth to make you think that you need to pay more in. Check these. Chances are it'll be based on pretty low growth. You always have the option to push the growth higher by investing in higher-risk funds too.

* Bear in mind that as you get older, you will probably earn more, meaning that it will be easier for both you and your employer to contribute more.

* As you approach retirement, the chances are you'll have some disposable income that will allow you to increase your contributions.

* You probably won't need as much to live on when you retire unless you plan on still having big debts or going out frequently with friends.

* Annuity rates are usually fairly low, and again, a pension calculator might make a number of assumptions about the annuity you buy - check these. There are plenty of other options these days, such as drawdown policies that will allow you to avoid buying an annuity altogether.

* All pensions offer a tax-free lump sum of 25% of your pension pot upon retirement, so any calculation will usually assume that you have taken this. For many people, this can be £100k+ if they've done a reasonable job of saving. Of course, you could spend this on something extravagant, but you could instead keep it in your overall pot and buy an annuity that's worth a lot more, invest in a rental property, or whatever.

* Bear in mind you may well get on the property ladder eventually, and find that by the time you retire, the family home you eventually achieved becomes too big after your children leave home - giving you the opportunity to downsize and bank a significant amount of equity.

All that said, yeah, if you want a comfortable retirement in the style to which you will likely become accustomed, then it is a lot of money to save for a very long time. Starting early is always a good plan; even if you're only saving a bit, it'll put you way ahead of where you might be otherwise.
